pos: n. (a lodging place; rendering Greek kataluma and pandocheion)
etymology: Old English inn, a dwelling. Two inns matter in the Gospels: one with no room, and one where a stranger paid for a wounded man's care.
biblical_def: An inn is a lodging place. Luke records the first: Mary “brought forth her firstborn son… and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn” (Luk 2:7). The second belongs to the good Samaritan, who “brought him to an inn, and took care of him” and paid the host to continue (Luk 10:34–35). In Genesis the brothers open their sacks at the inn and find the money returned (Gen 42:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inn as a house for the lodging and entertainment of travelers; and in England, a college of municipal or common law professors.
webster_full: INN, n. A house for the lodging and entertainment of travelers.
2. In England, a college of municipal or common law professors and students.
scriptures: And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
And went to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and set him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
And on the morrow when he departed, he took out two pence, and gave them to the host, and said unto him, Take care of him; and whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee.
And as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the inn, he espied his money; for, behold, it was in his sack's mouth.
corruption_summary: Christmas sentiment blames an innkeeper who is never mentioned, while Luke simply records that there was no room — a fact about a crowded town, and a parable about a crowded world.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke names no innkeeper and assigns no blame; he says there was no room for them in the inn. The town was full because of a Roman census, and the arrangement that followed was ordinary rather than cruel — a manger in a place where animals were kept. What the detail supplies is a pattern the whole Gospel repeats: he came unto his own, and his own received him not. The absence of room is theological before it is sentimental.

The Samaritan's inn is the counterweight. He brought him to an inn, and took care of him, and on the morrow gave two pence to the host with an open-ended promise: whatsoever thou spendest more, when I come again, I will repay thee. Mercy in this parable is not a feeling at the roadside but a bill guaranteed at an inn by a man who intends to return.
roots_summary: Greek kataluma (G2646), a guest chamber or lodging — the same word for the upper room; pandocheion (G3829), a public inn.
roots_lines: Greek kataluma (G2646) — inn, guestchamber; Luke 2:7, and Mark 14:14 of the upper room.
Greek pandocheion (G3829) — inn; only Luke 10:34, with pandocheus, the host, in 10:35.
Hebrew malon (H4411) — lodging place; Genesis 42:27, 43:21.
usage: “There was no room for them in the inn” — a crowded town and a crowded world.
“Brought him to an inn, and took care of him” — mercy that pays a bill.
“When I come again, I will repay thee” — an open-ended guarantee.

pos: n. (a flat roof; rendering Hebrew gag, Greek doma)
etymology: House with top. Palestinian roofs were flat and usable — a room without walls, for sleeping, praying, drying flax, and being overheard.
biblical_def: A housetop is a flat roof. Christ commands proclamation from it: “what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops” (Mat 10:27). Peter goes up “upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour” and receives the vision that opens the gospel to Gentiles (Act 10:9). Proverbs twice prefers a corner of one to a house shared with strife (Pro 21:9; 25:24), and the psalmist is “as a sparrow alone upon the house top” (Psa 102:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines housetop as the top or roof of a house.
webster_full: HOUSETOP, n. The top or roof of a house.
scriptures: What I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops.
On the morrow, as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour:
It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.
I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.
corruption_summary: Private conviction is prized and public declaration avoided, and Christ's instruction runs the other way — what is given in the ear is to be preached on the roof.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 10:27 describes a transfer: what I tell you in darkness, that speak ye in light: and what ye hear in the ear, that preach ye upon the housetops. Private instruction exists for public proclamation. The disciples were not given secret knowledge to keep but a message to relay at volume, and the housetop was the loudest available platform in a village. A Christianity that receives in the ear and never reaches the roof has kept half the instruction.

Peter's rooftop matters for the opposite reason. He went up to pray, alone, hungry, at noon — and the vision that came reordered the entire mission of the church. Ordinary devotional habit, kept at an ordinary hour, was where the Gentile door opened. Neither the housetop nor the hour was remarkable; he was simply there.
roots_summary: Hebrew gag (H1406), a flat roof; Greek doma (G1430), a housetop — a usable outdoor room in both Testaments.
roots_lines: Hebrew gag (H1406) — roof, housetop; Deuteronomy 22:8, Joshua 2:6, Proverbs 21:9.
Greek doma (G1430) — housetop; Matthew 10:27, Acts 10:9, Luke 12:3.
usage: “Preach ye upon the housetops” — the ear receives, the roof declares.
“Peter went up upon the housetop to pray” — an ordinary habit, an extraordinary vision.
“Better to dwell in a corner of the housetop” — the roof preferred to a house with strife.

pos: n. (a pit prison; rendering Hebrew bor, a cistern)
etymology: From Old French donjon. The Hebrew word is simply a pit or cistern — men were held in empty water-tanks, which is exactly the horror.
biblical_def: A dungeon is a pit prison. Jeremiah is let down by cords into one with no water, “but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire” (Jer 38:6), and rescued by an Ethiopian eunuch who fetches old rags to pad the ropes (Jer 38:11–13). Joseph is brought “hastily out of the dungeon” to stand before Pharaoh (Gen 41:14). Paul and Silas are thrust into the inner prison at Philippi and sing at midnight (Act 16:24–25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dungeon as a close prison, or a deep, dark place of confinement.
webster_full: DUNGEON, n. A close prison, or a deep, dark place of confinement.
DUNGEON, v.t. To confine in a dungeon.
scriptures: Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire.

So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah.
Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.
And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.
corruption_summary: Faithfulness is expected to be rewarded promptly, and Scripture keeps putting its most faithful men at the bottom of pits for telling the truth.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah was in the mire for preaching what God gave him to preach, and his rescue came from an unexpected quarter — Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a foreigner and a eunuch, who told the king plainly that the princes had done evil. The detail Scripture preserves is his kindness in the method: he took old cast clouts and rotten rags and let them down by cords, and told Jeremiah to put them under his armholes. A man being pulled from a pit could still be injured by the ropes, and someone thought about it.

Acts 16 shows the other response. Beaten, with feet in the stocks, in the inner prison, Paul and Silas prayed and sang praises unto God at midnight — and the prisoners heard them. The audience is worth noticing. Their singing was not private consolation; it was overheard by men in the same dark, and the jailer who later asked what must I do to be saved had a night's worth of evidence about what these men actually believed.
roots_summary: Hebrew bor (H953), a pit or cistern; tsinoq and bayith kele, prison house; Greek esoteros phulake, the inner prison of Acts 16:24.
roots_lines: Hebrew bor (H953) — pit, cistern, dungeon; Jeremiah 38:6, Genesis 37:24 of Joseph's pit.
Hebrew tit (H2916) — mire, clay; Jeremiah 38:6, Jeremiah sunk in the mire.
usage: “There was no water in the dungeon, but mire” — a cistern used as a cell.
“Put now these old cast clouts… under thine armholes” — kindness in the method of rescue.
“At midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang… and the prisoners heard them” — an audience in the dark.

pos: n. (a way in; also a beginning; rendering Hebrew pethach, Greek eisodos)
etymology: From Latin intrare, to enter. Scripture uses entrance for doorways, for the beginning of a work, and for the reception of light.
biblical_def: An entrance is a way in. The psalmist makes it a picture of understanding: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130). Paul recalls his reception at Thessalonica — “ye yourselves know our entrance in unto you, that it was not in vain” (1Th 2:1) — and Peter promises “an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom” (2Pe 1:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines entrance as the act of entering into a place; the power of entering; the door, gate, passage or avenue by which a place may be entered; and the beginning of any thing.
webster_full: ENTRANCE, n. The act of entering into a place; as the entrance of a person into a house.
2. The power of entering.
3. The door, gate, passage or avenue, by which a place may be entered.
4. Commencement; initiation; beginning.
scriptures: The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
For yourselves, brethren, know our entrance in unto you, that it was not in vain:
For so an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.
NUN. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
corruption_summary: Scripture is treated as requiring expertise before it can help, and Psalm 119 says its mere entrance gives light and understanding to the simple.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 119:130 is the charter of every plain reader: the entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple. The light does not wait on a commentary or a degree; it begins where the words get in. That is not an argument against study — the same psalm is 176 verses of sustained meditation — but it settles who Scripture is for. The simple are not a category to be handed a simplified version; they are the ones explicitly promised understanding.

Peter's use is worth pairing with it. An entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom follows a list of virtues to be added to faith, and the promise is not bare admission but an abundant entrance. The picture is not of a believer scraping in but of one welcomed with room to spare.
roots_summary: Hebrew pethach (H6608), an opening or entrance; Greek eisodos (G1529), a way in, an entering.
roots_lines: Hebrew pethach (H6608) — opening, entrance; Psalm 119:130.
Greek eisodos (G1529) — entrance, coming in; 1 Thessalonians 1:9, 2:1, 2 Peter 1:11, Hebrews 10:19.
usage: “The entrance of thy words giveth light” — light begins where the words get in.
“Our entrance in unto you… was not in vain” — Paul on his reception.
“An entrance… ministered unto you abundantly” — welcomed with room to spare.

pos: n. (a public square; rendering Greek agora)
etymology: Market with place. The Greek agora was the town's civic centre — commerce, hiring, lawsuits, and idle standing all happened there.
biblical_def: A marketplace is a public square. It is where the householder finds men “standing idle in the marketplace” and sends them into the vineyard (Mat 20:3). Christ likens His generation to “children sitting in the markets, and calling unto their fellows” who will neither dance nor mourn (Mat 11:16–17). He rebukes scribes who love greetings there (Mar 12:38), and Paul disputes daily in the Athenian market with them that met with him (Act 17:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines market-place as the place where provisions or goods are exposed for sale; a public place.
webster_full: MARKET-PLACE, n. The place where provisions or goods are exposed for sale.
MARKET, n. A public place in a city or town, where provisions or cattle are exposed for sale; a market-place.
scriptures: And he went out about the third hour, and saw others standing idle in the marketplace,
But whereunto shall I liken this generation? It is like unto children sitting in the markets, and calling unto their fellows,
Therefore disputed he in the synagogue with the Jews, and with the devout persons, and in the market daily with them that met with him.
And he said unto them in his doctrine, Beware of the scribes, which love to go in long clothing, and love salutations in the marketplaces,
corruption_summary: Christians debate whether to engage the public square, and Paul simply went there daily and reasoned with whoever turned up.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 17:17 describes a method rather than a strategy: therefore disputed he in the synagogue with the Jews, and with the devout persons, and in the market daily with them that met with him. The synagogue was the expected venue; the market was where everyone else was, and he treated both as ordinary. Not a campaign, not an event — daily, with whoever met with him. Athens' response was mixed, as it always is, and Luke records both the mockers and the ones that clave unto him and believed.

Matthew 11's picture of children in the markets is Christ's diagnosis of a generation that could not be pleased. We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented. John came fasting and was called demon-possessed; the Son of man came eating and was called a glutton. When the objection changes to fit whatever is offered, the objection was never the real issue.
roots_summary: Greek agora (G58), the marketplace or public square; agoraios (G60), of the marketplace — the loafers of Acts 17:5.
roots_lines: Greek agora (G58) — marketplace; Matthew 11:16, 20:3, Mark 12:38, Acts 17:17.
Greek agorazo (G59) — to buy in the market; 1 Corinthians 6:20, ye are bought with a price.
usage: “Standing idle in the marketplace” — where the eleventh-hour men were found.
“In the market daily with them that met with him” — Paul's ordinary method.
“Children sitting in the markets” — a generation that could not be pleased.

pos: n. pl. (granaries and treasuries; rendering Hebrew otsar and miskenoth)
etymology: Store with house. A storehouse holds what is not needed today — which makes it a test of both faith and generosity.
biblical_def: Storehouses hold reserves. Joseph opens Egypt's during the famine (Gen 41:56). Malachi makes one the site of a test: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven” (Mal 3:10). The psalmist notes that God “layeth up the depth in storehouses” (Psa 33:7), and Christ observes that the ravens have neither storehouse nor barn, yet God feedeth them (Luk 12:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines storehouse as a house in which things are stored; a magazine; a repository; a warehouse.
webster_full: STOREHOUSE, n. A house in which things are stored; a magazine; a repository; a warehouse.
2. A repository.
3. A great mass reposited.
scriptures: Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.
And the famine was over all the face of the earth: And Joseph opened all the storehouses, and sold unto the Egyptians; and the famine waxed sore in the land of Egypt. all the
He gathereth the waters of the sea together as an heap: he layeth up the depth in storehouses.
Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them: how much more are ye better than the fowls?
corruption_summary: Malachi's storehouse text is quoted for the promise and rarely for the invitation attached — prove me now herewith, which makes it an experiment rather than a formula.
corruption_paragraphs: Malachi 3:10 contains the only place in Scripture where God invites His people to test Him: prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it. The context is a nation robbing God while asking wherein have we robbed thee, and the storehouse exists so that there may be meat in mine house — the purpose is provision for the ministry, not the enrichment of the giver.

Luke 12:24 puts the storehouse in perspective without abolishing it. Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them: how much more are ye better than the fowls? Joseph filled granaries by divine instruction, so storing is not condemned. What is condemned, in the parable immediately before, is a man who built bigger barns and said to his soul, take thine ease, on the night his soul was required.
roots_summary: Hebrew otsar (H214), treasury, storehouse; miskenoth (H4543), store-cities — the ones Israel built for Pharaoh in Exodus 1:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew otsar (H214) — treasure, storehouse; Malachi 3:10, Psalm 33:7, Deuteronomy 28:12.
Hebrew miskenoth (H4543) — store-cities; Exodus 1:11, 2 Chronicles 8:4.
usage: “Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse… and prove me now” — the one invited test.
“That there may be meat in mine house” — the storehouse's stated purpose.
“Neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them” — the ravens as evidence.

pos: n. (a water channel; rendering Hebrew tealah)
etymology: From Latin conducere, to lead together. A conduit leads water where it would not naturally go — and Jerusalem's is the setting for a famous confrontation.
biblical_def: A conduit is a water channel. Isaiah is sent to meet Ahaz “at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field” (Isa 7:3) — where the king was inspecting his water supply ahead of a siege — and there receives the sign of Immanuel. Rabshakeh stands by the same conduit to taunt Hezekiah's men (2Ki 18:17). Hezekiah “made a pool, and a conduit, and brought water into the city” (2Ki 20:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conduit as a canal or pipe for the conveyance of water; an aqueduct; and a vessel that conveys the blood or other fluid.
webster_full: CONDUIT, n. A canal or pipe for the conveyance of water; an aqueduct.
2. A vessel that conveys the blood or other fluid.
3. A conductor.
scriptures: Then said the LORD unto Isaiah, Go forth now to meet Ahaz, thou, and Shearjashub thy son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field;

And the king of Assyria sent Tartan and Rabsaris and Rabshakeh from Lachish to king Hezekiah with a great host against Jerusalem. And they went up and came to Jerusalem. And when they were come up, they came and stood by the conduit of the upper pool, which is in the highway of the fuller's field.

And the rest of the acts of Hezekiah, and all his might, and how he made a pool, and a conduit, and brought water into the city, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
corruption_summary: Crisis drives leaders to inspect their resources, and God met Ahaz at the waterworks to offer him a sign he did not want.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 7 stages the encounter with care. Ahaz's heart was moved as the trees of the wood are moved with the wind, and he had gone out to check the water supply — the most practical possible response to an approaching siege. God sent Isaiah to meet him precisely there, told him to ask a sign as deep as hell or as high above, and Ahaz refused with a pious excuse: I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD. The refusal was unbelief dressed as reverence, and God gave the sign anyway: behold, a virgin shall conceive.

Hezekiah, at the same conduit a generation later, faced the same Assyrian threat and did the opposite — he took the threatening letter into the house of the LORD and spread it before Him. Two kings, one waterworks, and the difference between them is what they did with a crisis they could not engineer their way out of.
roots_summary: Hebrew tealah (H8585), a conduit or channel — the same word as Elijah's trench on Carmel.
roots_lines: Hebrew tealah (H8585) — conduit, watercourse, trench; Isaiah 7:3, 36:2, 2 Kings 18:17, 20:20.
Hebrew berekah (H1295) — pool; the upper pool at the conduit's end.
usage: “At the end of the conduit of the upper pool” — God meets a king at the waterworks.
“I will not ask, neither will I tempt the LORD” — unbelief dressed as reverence.
“Made a pool, and a conduit, and brought water into the city” — Hezekiah's engineering.

pos: n. (an upward slope; rendering Hebrew maaleh)
etymology: From Latin ascendere, to climb. Scripture's ascents are literal hills that carry weight — a king's grief, a queen's astonishment.
biblical_def: An ascent is an upward slope. David flees Absalom “by the ascent of mount Olivet, and wept as he went up” (2Sa 15:30). The queen of Sheba sees Solomon's wisdom, his house, his table, and “his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD” — and there was no more spirit in her (1Ki 10:5). The ascent of Akrabbim marks a boundary of the land (Num 34:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ascent as the act of rising; the way by which one ascends; an eminence or high place; and acclivity, the rise of a hill.
webster_full: ASCENT, n. The act of rising; motion upwards.
2. The way by which one ascends; the means of ascending.
3. An eminence, hill or high place.
4. Acclivity; the rise of a hill.
scriptures: And David went up by the ascent of mount Olivet, and wept as he went up, and had his head covered, and he went barefoot: and all the people that was with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went up. and

And the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD; there was no more spirit in her.

And your border shall turn from the south to the ascent of Akrabbim, and pass on to Zin: and the going forth thereof shall be from the south to Kadeshbarnea, and shall go on to Hazaraddar, and pass on to Azmon:
Howbeit I believed not the words, until I came, and mine eyes had seen it: and, behold, the half was not told me: thy wisdom and prosperity exceedeth the fame which I heard.
corruption_summary: Splendour is expected to persuade, and what finally overwhelmed the queen of Sheba was the way Solomon went up to worship.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 10:5 lists what the queen of Sheba saw in ascending order, and the last item is the one that undid her: the meat of his table, the sitting of his servants, the attendance of his ministers, their apparel, his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD. The wealth impressed her; the worship finished her. Her verdict was that the half had not been told, and she blessed the LORD who delighted in Solomon to set him on the throne.

The same hill road serves the opposite emotion in 2 Samuel. David went up by the ascent of mount Olivet, and wept as he went up, and had his head covered, and he went barefoot. A king climbing out of his capital in grief, and a queen climbing into it in wonder — and centuries later Another would weep over that city from the same slope.
roots_summary: Hebrew maaleh (H4608), an ascent or stairway — also the root behind the Songs of Degrees, the psalms of ascent.
roots_lines: Hebrew maaleh (H4608) — ascent, going up; 2 Samuel 15:30, 1 Kings 10:5, Numbers 34:4.
Hebrew maalah (H4609) — step, degree; the title of Psalms 120-134, songs of degrees.
usage: “Wept as he went up” — a king climbing out of his own city.
“His ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD” — the sight that finished a queen.
“The half was not told me” — her verdict.

pos: n. pl. (regions, districts; rendering Hebrew qatsah, Greek meros)
etymology: From Latin quartus, a fourth — the four directions, and so any region. The KJV uses it for territory rather than lodgings.
biblical_def: Quarters are regions. Peter passes “throughout all quarters” and comes to the saints at Lydda (Act 9:32). The law commands leaven be put away “out of all thy quarters” at Passover (Exo 13:7). Jeremiah warns of judgment coming “from the four quarters of heaven” (Jer 49:36), and Revelation speaks of nations “in the four quarters of the earth” (Rev 20:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines quarter as a fourth part; a region in the heavens, as the four cardinal points; and a particular region of a town, city or country.
webster_full: QUARTER, n. The fourth part; as the quarter of an hour.
2. A region in the heavens, as the four cardinal points.
3. A particular region of a town, city or country.
4. Proper station; specific place of duty.
scriptures: And it came to pass, as Peter passed throughout all quarters, he came down also to the saints which dwelt at Lydda.
Unleavened bread shall be eaten seven days; and there shall no leavened bread be seen with thee, neither shall there be leaven seen with thee in all thy quarters.
And upon Elam will I bring the four winds from the four quarters of heaven, and will scatter them toward all those winds; and there shall be no nation whither the outcasts of Elam shall not come.
And shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four quarters of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them together to battle: the number of whom is as the sand of the sea.
corruption_summary: Sin is dealt with where it is visible, and the Passover command reaches into all thy quarters — every corner of the property, not merely the table.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 13:7 makes the search total: there shall no leavened bread be seen with thee, neither shall there be leaven seen with thee in all thy quarters. Not merely absent from the meal — absent from the premises. Paul draws the application directly: purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump… for even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us. A congregation, like a house, has quarters where things accumulate unexamined.

Peter's travels in Acts 9:32 show the phrase's other use, and the pastoral habit behind it. It came to pass, as Peter passed throughout all quarters, he came down also to the saints which dwelt at Lydda. No campaign is described; he simply went through the regions visiting believers, and healings and a resurrection followed in two small towns nobody would have chosen for a headquarters.
roots_summary: Hebrew gebul (H1366), border, territory — rendered quarters in Exodus 13:7; Greek meros (G3313), a part or district.
roots_lines: Hebrew gebul (H1366) — border, coast, quarter; Exodus 13:7.
Greek meros (G3313) — part, region, quarter; Acts 9:32, 19:1, the upper coasts.
Greek gonia (G1137) — corner; Revelation 20:8, the four quarters of the earth.
usage: “Neither shall there be leaven seen with thee in all thy quarters” — a total search.
“As Peter passed throughout all quarters” — ordinary visiting, extraordinary results.
“The four quarters of the earth” — the whole compass gathered.

pos: n. (a valley; rendering Hebrew emeq and biqah)
etymology: From Latin vallis. The vale is low ground — fertile, defensible by chariots, and in Scripture often the place where things are decided.
biblical_def: A vale is a valley. The vale of Siddim, full of slimepits, is where the kings fight and Lot is taken (Gen 14:3,10). Solomon “made silver to be in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars made he to be as the sycomore trees that are in the vale” (1Ki 10:27). Joshua's conquest reaches “the vale, and the plains” (Jos 10:40), and the Philistines pitch in the valley of Elah where David meets Goliath (1Sa 17:2–3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vale as a tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley.
webster_full: VALE, n. A tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
scriptures: And the vale of Siddim was full of slimepits; and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, and fell there; and they that remained fled to the mountain.
And the king made silver to be in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars made he to be as the sycomore trees that are in the vale, for abundance.

So Joshua smote all the country of the hills, and of the south, and of the vale, and of the springs, and all their kings: he left none remaining, but utterly destroyed all that breathed, as the LORD God of Israel commanded.
And the Philistines stood on a mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on a mountain on the other side: and there was a valley between them.
corruption_summary: Low ground is treated as the place faith retreats from, and Scripture keeps staging its decisive encounters there rather than on the heights.
corruption_paragraphs: The valley of Elah is the pattern. Two armies stood on opposite mountains with the valley between them, and nothing happened for forty days because the space between was where the risk lay. David went down into it. Height is where armies feel safe; the low ground is where the matter is settled, and the shepherd who came with bread for his brothers was the only man willing to descend.

Genesis 14 supplies the warning attached. The vale of Siddim was full of slimepits, and the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled and fell there. Fertile low ground — the plain Lot had chosen because it was well watered everywhere — turned out to be treacherous underfoot. The most attractive valley in the story was the one that swallowed the men who ran into it.
roots_summary: Hebrew emeq (H6010), a valley or vale; biqah (H1237), a broad valley; shephelah (H8219), the lowland.
roots_lines: Hebrew emeq (H6010) — valley, vale; Genesis 14:3, 1 Samuel 17:2, Joshua 8:13.
Hebrew shephelah (H8219) — lowland, vale; Joshua 10:40, 1 Kings 10:27.
usage: “The vale of Siddim was full of slimepits” — attractive ground, treacherous underfoot.
“There was a valley between them” — where the matter is settled.
“Cedars… as the sycomore trees that are in the vale” — Solomon's abundance.

pos: n. pl. (colonnaded walkways; rendering Hebrew attiq and rahat)
etymology: From Italian galleria, a long covered passage. In Ezekiel's temple vision the galleries are tiered chambers; in the Song, a place of being held.
biblical_def: Galleries are colonnaded walkways or tiered chambers. Ezekiel's temple vision measures them in detail: “the galleries thereof were on the one side and on the other side” (Eze 42:3). The Song uses the word for the king's own space: “How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights! The king is held in the galleries” (Son 7:6–5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines gallery as a covered part of a building, commonly in the wings, used as an ambulatory or place for walking; and a balcony or platform.
webster_full: GALLERY, n. In architecture, a covered part of a building, commonly in the wings, used as an ambulatory or place for walking.
2. An ornamental apartment for works of art.
3. A balcony; a platform.
scriptures: Over against the twenty cubits which were for the inner court, and over against the pavement which was for the utter court, was gallery against gallery in three stories.
Thine head upon thee is like Carmel, and the hair of thine head like purple; the king is held in the galleries.

And he measured the length of the building over against the separate place which was behind it, and the galleries thereof on the one side and on the other side, an hundred cubits, with the inner temple, and the porches of the court;
Now the upper chambers were shorter: for the galleries were higher than these, than the lower, and than the middlemost of the building.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel's measurements are skipped as tedious, when the point of a vision given to exiles was that the house had exact dimensions and would exist.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 40-42 is nine chapters of measurements given to a man in exile whose temple lay in rubble. A vision of the ruins would have been news; a vision of galleries measured to the cubit was a promise. The tedium is the theology — God describing rooms, walkways, and thicknesses with the precision of a builder who intends to build. Exiles do not need sentiment about the future; they need dimensions.

The Song's line is one of the few places Scripture pictures the King as willingly held. The king is held in the galleries — not detained, but stayed, by delight in His bride. Set beside Ezekiel's architecture, the two uses form a whole: a house measured for His presence, and a King who does not want to leave it.
roots_summary: Hebrew attiq (H862), a gallery or terraced chamber; rahat (H7298), a trough or gallery, in Song 7:5.
roots_lines: Hebrew attiq (H862) — gallery; Ezekiel 41:15-16, 42:3, 5.
Hebrew rahat (H7298) — gallery, trough; Song of Solomon 7:5, Genesis 30:38.
usage: “The galleries thereof were on the one side and on the other” — dimensions given to exiles.
“The king is held in the galleries” — stayed by delight.
“Gallery against gallery in three stories” — a house described as buildable.

pos: n. (a large room, a courtyard; rendering Greek aule and praitorion)
etymology: Old English heall. In the Gospels the hall is where two things happen at once — a trial inside, and a denial by the fire.
biblical_def: A hall is a large room or courtyard. Peter sits “without in the palace” and follows Christ “unto the high priest's palace, and went in, and sat with the servants, to see the end” (Mat 26:58). Luke names the setting of the denial: “when they had kindled a fire in the midst of the hall, and were set down together, Peter sat down among them” (Luk 22:55). Soldiers lead Christ “into the hall, called Praetorium” and mock Him there (Mar 15:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hall as a large room at the entrance of a house or public building; and a court of justice, or the room in which courts are held.
webster_full: HALL, n. In architecture, a large room at the entrance of a house or public building.
2. An apartment for the reception of company.
3. A court of justice, or the room in which courts are held.
4. A manor-house, in which courts were formerly held.
scriptures: And when they had kindled a fire in the midst of the hall, and were set down together, Peter sat down among them.
But Peter followed him afar off unto the high priest's palace, and went in, and sat with the servants, to see the end.
And the soldiers led him away into the hall, called Praetorium; and they call together the whole band.
And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.
corruption_summary: Failure is imagined as happening far from Christ, and Peter's denial occurred close enough that the Lord turned and looked upon him.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke gives the detail the other Gospels do not: and the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word of the Lord… and Peter went out, and wept bitterly. The denial happened within sight-line of the trial. Peter had followed further than any other disciple — that is why he was in the hall at all — and his failure occurred at the exact point his courage had carried him. The men who ran had nothing to deny.

The fire in the midst of the hall is worth noticing too. Peter sat down among them, warming himself at the enemies' fire on a cold night, and the questions came from people beside him in the light. Proximity to danger is survivable; comfort in the wrong company is what loosened his tongue.
roots_summary: Greek aule (G833), courtyard, hall — the same word as the sheepfold in John 10; praitorion (G4232), the governor's residence.
roots_lines: Greek aule (G833) — hall, courtyard, palace; Matthew 26:58, 69, Luke 22:55.
Greek praitorion (G4232) — Praetorium, judgment hall; Mark 15:16, John 18:28, 33.
usage: “A fire in the midst of the hall… Peter sat down among them” — warmed at the enemies' fire.
“Sat with the servants, to see the end” — he followed further than the rest.
“The Lord turned, and looked upon Peter” — the denial was within sight.

pos: n. (a sleeping room; rendering Hebrew chadar mishkab)
etymology: Bed with chamber. In Scripture the bedchamber is where a child is hidden, a king is killed, and a heart is examined.
biblical_def: A bedchamber is a sleeping room. Jehosheba hides the infant Joash “in the bedchamber, from Athaliah, so that he was not slain” (2Ki 11:2) — preserving the line of David through a coup. Ish-bosheth is murdered on his bed “in his bedchamber” (2Sa 4:7). Ecclesiastes warns, “curse not the king… nor the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice” (Ecc 10:20), and the psalmist commands, “commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still” (Psa 4:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bedchamber as an apartment or chamber intended or appropriated for a bed, or for sleep and repose.
webster_full: BEDCHAMBER, n. An apartment or chamber intended or appropriated for a bed, or for sleep and repose.
scriptures: But Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him from among the king's sons which were slain; and they hid him, even him and his nurse, in the bedchamber from Athaliah, so that he was not slain.
For when they came into the house, he lay on his bed in his bedchamber, and they smote him, and slew him, and beheaded him, and took his head, and gat them away through the plain all night.
Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.
corruption_summary: Private speech is assumed to be safe, and Ecclesiastes warns that a bird of the air shall carry the voice out of the bedchamber.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Kings 11 turns on a woman and a bedroom. Athaliah destroyed all the seed royal, but Jehosheba took Joash from among the king's sons which were slain, and hid him in the bedchamber — and the covenant line of David survived six years in a back room of the temple because one aunt acted. The whole promise of a son of David on the throne hung, humanly speaking, on that hiding place.

Psalm 4:4 gives the bedchamber its best use: stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. The place where a person is finally alone and unobserved is where honest self-examination is possible — and the psalm pairs it with stillness rather than with anxious review. Ecclesiastes' warning and the psalm's counsel fit together: watch what you say there, and use it to listen.
roots_summary: Hebrew chadar (H2315), a chamber; with mishkab (H4904), a bed — the compound gives bedchamber.
roots_lines: Hebrew chadar mishkab (H2315/H4904) — bedchamber; 2 Kings 11:2, 2 Samuel 4:7, Exodus 8:3.
Hebrew damam (H1826) — to be still, silent; Psalm 4:4, commune with your own heart… and be still.
usage: “Hid him… in the bedchamber, from Athaliah” — the line of David preserved in a back room.
“A bird of the air shall carry the voice” — private speech is not safe.
“Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still” — the room's best use.

pos: n. pl. (limits, extremities; rendering Hebrew totsaah)
etymology: Out with going. The word marks where a boundary runs out — the point at which a territory ends and something else begins.
biblical_def: Outgoings are boundary extremities. Joshua's land allotments use the word constantly: “the outgoings thereof were at the sea” (Jos 16:8), “the outgoings of it were at Jordan” (Jos 16:7). The psalmist lifts it into praise: God “maketh the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice” (Psa 65:8) — the far edges of the day, east and west, made glad.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines outgoing as the act of going out; and outgoings as utmost border, extreme limit.
webster_full: OUTGOING, n. The act of going out.
2. The state of going out.
3. Utmost border; extreme limit.
scriptures: They also that dwell in the uttermost parts are afraid at thy tokens: thou makest the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice.
The border went out from Tappuah westward unto the river Kanah; and the goings out thereof were at the sea. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Ephraim by their families.
And it went down from Janohah to Ataroth, and to Naarath, and came to Jericho, and went out at Jordan.

And the coast descended unto the river Kanah, southward of the river: these cities of Ephraim are among the cities of Manasseh: the coast of Manasseh also was on the north side of the river, and the outgoings of it were at the sea: river
corruption_summary: Genealogies and boundary lists are skipped as filler, and they are the legal record that a promise about land was actually kept.
corruption_paragraphs: The outgoings in Joshua are surveyor's language, and their tedium is their point. God had promised a land; Joshua records which brook, which hill, and where each tribe's border ran out. A promise fulfilled in general terms would have been unverifiable, and these chapters make it a matter of record — there failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass.

Psalm 65:8 takes the same word somewhere unexpected. Thou makest the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice — the outermost edges of the day, where the sun comes up and goes down, are described as glad. The furthest limits of anything God has made are not empty margins; they are singing.
roots_summary: Hebrew totsaah (H8444), an outgoing, extremity, border — also used of the issues of life in Proverbs 4:23.
roots_lines: Hebrew totsaah (H8444) — outgoing, border, issue; Joshua 16:3-8, 17:9, Psalm 65:8.
Proverbs 4:23 uses the same noun — out of the heart are the issues of life.
usage: “The outgoings thereof were at the sea” — a promise recorded as survey.
“The outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice” — the day's far edges singing.
“Out of it are the issues of life” — the same word, of the heart.

pos: n. pl. (fords and mountain crossings; rendering Hebrew maabar)
etymology: From pass. A passage is a crossing point — a ford, a pass, the one place an army or a fugitive can get through.
biblical_def: Passages are crossing points. Jephthah's men take the passages of Jordan and use the word Shibboleth to identify fleeing Ephraimites (Jdg 12:5–6). Jonathan and his armourbearer climb between two sharp rocks “in the passages” to reach the Philistine garrison (1Sa 14:4). Jeremiah reports of fallen Babylon that “the passages are stopped” (Jer 51:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines passage as the act of passing; a road, way or avenue by which men or animals may pass; and a narrow way.
webster_full: PASSAGE, n. The act of passing or moving by land or water, or through the air.
2. The time of passing.
3. Road; way; avenue; a place where men or beasts may pass.
4. Entrance or exit.
scriptures: And the Gileadites took the passages of Jordan before the Ephraimites: and it was so, that when those Ephraimites which were escaped said, Let me go over; that the men of Gilead said unto him, Art thou an Ephraimite? If he said, Nay;

Then said they unto him, Say now Shibboleth: and he said Sibboleth: for he could not frame to pronounce it right. Then they took him, and slew him at the passages of Jordan: and there fell at that time of the Ephraimites forty and two thousand.

And between the passages, by which Jonathan sought to go over unto the Philistines' garrison, there was a sharp rock on the one side, and a sharp rock on the other side: and the name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh.
And that the passages are stopped, and the reeds they have burned with fire, and the men of war are affrighted.
corruption_summary: Identity is asserted and rarely tested, and at Jordan's passages a single mispronounced syllable decided who lived.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 12 is a grim story about a shibboleth — a word Ephraimites could not pronounce. Forty-two thousand died at the fords, identified by an accent they could not disguise. It is the Bible's own example of a test that measures tribe rather than truth, and it stands as a warning about every party marker a church erects: a password that sorts by dialect will always kill some of the wrong people.

Jonathan's passage runs the other way. He and his armourbearer climbed on hands and feet between two sharp rocks, saying, it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few. Two men took a route an army could not use, and the ground the enemy thought impassable was exactly where God gave the victory.
roots_summary: Hebrew maabar (H4569), a ford or pass; maabarah (H4569), a crossing place — the fords of Jordan.
roots_lines: Hebrew maabarah (H4569) — ford, passage; Judges 12:5-6, Isaiah 10:29, Jeremiah 51:32.
Hebrew shibboleth (H7641) — an ear of grain, or a stream; Judges 12:6, the test word.
usage: “The Gileadites took the passages of Jordan” — a crossing turned into a checkpoint.
“Say now Shibboleth” — a test that measured accent, not loyalty.
“There was a sharp rock on the one side” — Jonathan's impassable route.

pos: n. pl. (fallen remains; rendering Hebrew harisuth)
etymology: From Latin ruere, to fall. Ruins are what a building becomes; Scripture's interest is chiefly in who rebuilds them.
biblical_def: Ruins are fallen remains. Amos prophesies restoration in exactly these terms: “In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old” (Amo 9:11) — a text James quotes at the Jerusalem council to justify receiving Gentiles (Act 15:16). Isaiah promises that they shall “build the old wastes… and they shall repair the waste cities” (Isa 61:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ruin as destruction; fall; overthrow; defeat; and the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house, fortress, or any work of men.
webster_full: RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; defeat; that change of any thing which destroys it, or entirely defeats its object.
2. The remains of a decayed or demolished city, house, fortress, or any work of men or of nature.
3. The state of being destroyed; the state of being decayed or having lost its former excellence.
scriptures: In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old:
After this I will return, and will build again the tabernacle of David, which is fallen down; and I will build again the ruins thereof, and I will set it up:
And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.

But he that heareth, and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth; against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great.
corruption_summary: Restoration is imagined as replacement, and both Amos and Isaiah promise something stranger — the old ruins themselves raised and repaired.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 9:11 is precise about the material: I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old. Not a new tabernacle on a clear site — the fallen thing raised. James used this at the Jerusalem council to explain why Gentiles were streaming in without becoming Jews: the rebuilding of David's fallen tent was always meant to include the residue of men, and the nations, upon whom my name is called.

Isaiah 61:4 assigns the work to the very people who had been comforted: they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations. The mourners of Zion, given beauty for ashes, become the builders. That is the pattern — those who have been restored are the ones handed the trowel.
roots_summary: Hebrew harisuth (H2034), ruins; haras (H2040), to tear down; Greek kataskapto (G2679), to dig down, in Acts 15:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew harisuth (H2034) — ruins; only Amos 9:11.
Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — waste, desolation; Isaiah 61:4, the old wastes.
Greek kataskapto (G2679) — ruined, dug down; Acts 15:16.
usage: “I will raise up his ruins” — the fallen thing rebuilt, not replaced.
“They shall repair the waste cities” — the comforted handed the trowel.
“The ruin of that house was great” — the house built without a foundation.

pos: n. (a round or route; rendering Hebrew tequphah and sabab)
etymology: From Latin circuire, to go around. A circuit is a route that returns to its start — the sun's, a judge's, or the wind's.
biblical_def: A circuit is a round. The psalmist describes the sun: “his going forth is from the end of the heaven, and his circuit unto the ends of it: and there is nothing hid from the heat thereof” (Psa 19:6). Samuel “went from year to year in circuit to Bethel, and Gilgal, and Mizpeh, and judged Israel in all those places” (1Sa 7:16). Job's friend says God “walketh in the circuit of heaven” (Job 22:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines circuit as the act of moving or passing round; the space enclosed in a circle, or within certain limits; and the visitation of judges for holding courts of justice.
webster_full: CIRCUIT, n. The act of moving or passing round; as the periodical circuit of the earth round the sun.
2. The space enclosed in a circle, or within certain limits.
3. Any space or extent measured round.
4. In England, the journey of judges for holding courts of justice.
scriptures: His going forth is from the end of the heaven, and his circuit unto the ends of it: and there is nothing hid from the heat thereof.
And he went from year to year in circuit to Bethel, and Gilgal, and Mizpeh, and judged Israel in all those places. in
Thick clouds are a covering to him, that he seeth not; and he walketh in the circuit of heaven.
Their line is gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In them hath he set a tabernacle for the sun,
corruption_summary: Ministry is drawn toward centres, and Samuel's practice was a yearly circuit to three towns so that justice came to people who could not travel.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 7:16-17 records a working pattern rather than an event: he went from year to year in circuit to Bethel, and Gilgal, and Mizpeh, and judged Israel in all those places. And his return was to Ramah; for there was his house; and there he judged Israel; and there he built an altar unto the LORD. A circuit, a home base, and an altar. Justice travelled to the people, and the judge who administered it worshipped where he lived.

Psalm 19 sets the sun's circuit beside the law of the LORD, and the join is deliberate. Nothing is hid from the heat of the one; nothing is hid from the searching of the other. The psalm moves from the sky's silent testimony to the written word to the psalmist's own secret faults, and the last request follows naturally: cleanse thou me from secret faults.
roots_summary: Hebrew tequphah (H8622), a circuit or revolution; sabab (H5437), to go around; chug (H2329), a circle, as of the heavens.
roots_lines: Hebrew tequphah (H8622) — circuit, revolution; Psalm 19:6, Exodus 34:22.
Hebrew sabab (H5437) — to go about, circuit; 1 Samuel 7:16.
Hebrew chug (H2329) — circle, compass; Job 22:14, Isaiah 40:22, the circle of the earth.
usage: “His circuit unto the ends of it” — nothing hid from the heat.
“From year to year in circuit… and judged Israel” — justice that travels.
“He walketh in the circuit of heaven” — Job's friend on God's compass.

pos: n. pl. (fixed limits; rendering Hebrew gebulah, Greek horothesia)
etymology: From Old French bonde, a limit. A bound is a line that may not be crossed — set by God for seas, nations, and lifespans alike.
biblical_def: Bounds are fixed limits. God sets them for the sea: “Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed” (Job 38:11), and for man's days: “his days are determined… thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass” (Job 14:5). Paul makes them the frame of history: God “hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; that they should seek the Lord” (Act 17:26–27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bound as a limit; the line which comprehends the whole of any given object or space; and boundary.
webster_full: BOUND, n. A limit; the line which comprehends the whole of any given object or space.
2. A limit by which any excursion is restrained; the limit of indulgence or desire.
BOUNDARY, n. A limit; a bound.
scriptures: And said, Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed?
Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass;
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us:
corruption_summary: Limits are experienced as insults to potential, and Acts 17 gives them a purpose — the bounds of habitation were set so that men should seek the Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 17:26-27 makes the boldest claim in Scripture about history and geography: God hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us. When and where a person is born are not accidents but arrangements, and the stated purpose of the arrangement is that he should seek God.

Job 38:11 is the sea's boundary and the most quotable sentence in the divine speeches: hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed. It is addressed to the most obviously uncontrollable thing in the ancient world. For a man in Job's position — whose life had been overrun by forces he could not check — the point is that even the sea has a line drawn for it, by Someone.
roots_summary: Hebrew gebulah (H1367), a boundary; choq (H2706), a decreed limit; Greek horothesia (G3734), a fixed boundary — only in Acts 17:26.
roots_lines: Hebrew gebulah (H1367) — boundary, border; Job 38:10, Psalm 104:9.
Hebrew choq (H2706) — decree, appointed limit; Job 14:5, 38:10.
Greek horothesia (G3734) — a setting of boundaries; only Acts 17:26.
usage: “Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further” — a line drawn for the sea.
“Thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass” — the limit of a life.
“The bounds of their habitation; that they should seek the Lord” — the stated purpose.

pos: n. (a shallow river crossing; rendering Hebrew maabar)
etymology: Old English ford. A ford is where a river can be crossed on foot — and Jabbok's is where a patriarch was left alone and renamed.
biblical_def: A ford is a shallow crossing. Jacob's night at the Jabbok begins with one: “he rose up that night… and passed over the ford Jabbok… and Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day” (Gen 32:22–24). Israel takes the fords of Jordan against Moab (Jdg 3:28), and Joshua's spies are pursued toward them (Jos 2:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ford as a place in a river or other water, where it may be passed by man or beast on foot, by wading.
webster_full: FORD, n. A place in a river or other water, where it may be passed by man or beast on foot, or by wading.
2. A stream; a current.
FORD, v.t. To pass or cross a river or other water by wading.
scriptures: And he rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two womenservants, and his eleven sons, and passed over the ford Jabbok.
And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day.

And he said unto them, Follow after me: for the LORD hath delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand. And they went down after him, and took the fords of Jordan toward Moab, and suffered not a man to pass over.
And he said, Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed. Israel: that is, A prince of God
corruption_summary: Transformation is sought in company and in daylight, and Jacob's came alone, at night, at a river crossing, and left him limping.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 32 is careful about the sequence. Jacob sent everything he had over the ford — wives, children, herds, all his substance — and then Jacob was left alone. The man who had spent his life arranging outcomes had finally arranged everything and had nothing left to manage. That is when the wrestling began, and it lasted until daybreak.

The outcome was a new name and a permanent limp: thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed. And the sun rose upon him, and he halted upon his thigh. Prevailing and being disabled in the same night is the shape of the encounter, and he named the place Peniel — I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.
roots_summary: Hebrew maabar (H4569), a ford or crossing; Yabboq (H2999), Jabbok — a name close to the verb for wrestling, abaq.
roots_lines: Hebrew maabar (H4569) — ford, passage; Genesis 32:22, Joshua 2:7, Judges 3:28.
Hebrew abaq (H79) — to wrestle, grapple; Genesis 32:24-25, only here in Scripture.
usage: “Passed over the ford Jabbok” — everything sent ahead.
“And Jacob was left alone” — nothing left to arrange.
“He halted upon his thigh” — prevailing and limping in one night.

pos: n. (a territory; rendering Greek chora and perichoros)
etymology: From Latin regio, a direction or territory. In the Gospels the region is the area a message reaches — and Luke tracks it carefully.
biblical_def: A region is a territory. Matthew applies Isaiah's prophecy to Christ's base of ministry: “the people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up” (Mat 4:16). John's preaching goes out “into all the region round about Jordan” (Luk 3:3), and after the synagogue at Nazareth “there went out a fame of him through all the region round about” (Luk 4:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines region as a tract of land or space of indefinite extent, usually a tract of considerable extent; a country; a division.
webster_full: REGION, n. A tract of land or space of indefinite extent, usually a tract of considerable extent.
2. The inhabitants of a region or district of country.
3. A part of the body.
scriptures: The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.
And he came into all the country about Jordan, preaching the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins;
And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee: and there went out a fame of him through all the region round about.
And the word of the Lord was published throughout all the region.
corruption_summary: Influence is measured by platform rather than by region, and Luke keeps reporting how far a message actually travelled through ordinary people talking.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke's phrase is repeated because he is tracking something: the fame of him went out through all the region round about. No campaign, no infrastructure — a rumour spreading through villages by word of mouth after He taught in their synagogues. Acts 13:49 uses the same construction: and the word of the Lord was published throughout all the region. Regional saturation in the New Testament happens by transmission rather than by broadcast.

Matthew 4:16 explains why the location mattered. Galilee of the Gentiles was the despised northern district, the region and shadow of death, and it is where the light is said to have sprung up. Christ based His ministry in the part of the country Jerusalem looked down on, and the prophecy He fulfilled had named that region seven centuries earlier.
roots_summary: Greek chora (G5561), a region or country; perichoros (G4066), the region round about — Luke's favourite phrase for spreading news.
roots_lines: Greek chora (G5561) — region, country; Matthew 4:16, Luke 2:8, Acts 13:49.
Greek perichoros (G4066) — region round about; Luke 3:3, 4:14, 7:17, Matthew 3:5.
usage: “The region and shadow of death” — where the light sprang up.
“All the region round about Jordan” — John's reach.
“The word of the Lord was published throughout all the region” — saturation by transmission.
